title: Recursion Practice
learningGoals: write recursive Fibonacci, power and sum-of-digits functions using the base case + smaller problem recipe
trace a recursive call tree by hand
explain why naive recursive Fibonacci is slow (repeated calls) and switch to a loop when speed matters

youtube.title: Recursion Practice: Fibonacci, Power, Digits | C Programming EP 40
youtube.description: Three classic recursion problems that show up in every C exam: Fibonacci, power and sum of digits. We solve each with the same three-step recipe, then discover why fib(40) makes over 33 crore function calls, and fix it with a simple loop. Chapters: 0:00 Mirror inside a mirror · 0:20 The recursion recipe · 0:50 Fibonacci · 2:00 Power · 2:45 Sum of digits · 3:45 Running it · 4:10 Bug of the Day: slow recursion · 5:50 Challenge

thumbnail.pose: Xecxec buried under tiny function cards

scenes.onScreen: Two mirrors facing each other: endless reflections of Xecxec getting smaller
scenes.narration: Stand between two mirrors in a shop in Margao, and you see yourself, inside yourself, inside yourself, smaller and smaller. Recursion feels like that. Last episode we learned the idea. Today we practise on three problems that appear in almost every C exam.

scenes.onScreen: Recipe card: 1. Smallest case? 2. How is the problem a smaller copy? 3. Combine
scenes.animation: Three steps tick in one by one
scenes.narration: For every recursion problem, ask three questions. One: what is the smallest case, where I already know the answer? That's the base case. Two: how is my problem a smaller copy of itself? Three: how do I combine the smaller answer into the full answer? Let's use this recipe three times.

scenes.onScreen: `practice.c` lines 3–8: fib, plus call tree for fib(4)
scenes.animation: Butter highlights; call tree grows branch by branch
scenes.narration: The Fibonacci series goes 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. Each number is the sum of the two before it. Recipe. Smallest case: fib of 0 is 0, fib of 1 is 1. Smaller copy: fib of n is fib of n minus 1 plus fib of n minus 2. [HL 3] Line three: int fib, int n. [HL 4-5] Lines four and five: if n is less than or equal to 1, return n. That one line covers both base cases, because fib of 0 is 0 and fib of 1 is 1. [HL 7] Line seven: return fib of n minus 1, plus fib of n minus 2. This function calls itself twice. Look at the call tree for fib of 4. It calls fib of 3 and fib of 2. fib of 3 calls fib of 2 and fib of 1. And see, fib of 2 appears twice. fib of 1 appears three times. Remember that; it matters soon.

scenes.animation: Butter highlights; tracker for exp counting down
scenes.narration: Next: power. 2 to the power 10. Recipe. Smallest case: anything to the power zero is 1. Smaller copy: base to the power exp is base times base to the power exp minus 1. [HL 10] Line ten: int power, int base, int exp. [HL 11-12] Lines eleven and twelve: if exp equals zero, return 1. [HL 14] Line fourteen: return base times power of base, exp minus 1. [TRACK exp=10] exp goes 10, 9, 8, all the way [TRACK exp=0] to 0, then the answers multiply back up to 1024.

scenes.animation: Digits of 4031 peel off one by one with % and / labels
scenes.narration: Third: sum of the digits of 4031. That's 4 plus 0 plus 3 plus 1, which is 8. Two tricks from EP 15: n mod 10 gives the last digit, and n divided by 10 removes the last digit. Recipe. Smallest case: if n is 0, there are no digits left, so the sum is 0. Smaller copy: the last digit plus the sum of the digits of the rest. [HL 17] Line seventeen: int sumDigits, int n. [HL 18-19] If n equals zero, return zero. [HL 21] Return n mod 10, plus sumDigits of n divided by 10. [TRACK n=4031] 4031 gives 1, plus sumDigits of 403. [TRACK n=403] That gives 3, plus sumDigits of 40. [TRACK n=40] That gives 0, plus sumDigits of 4. [TRACK n=4] That gives 4, plus sumDigits of 0, [TRACK n=0] which is 0. Total: 1 plus 3 plus 0 plus 4. 8.
Compile and run. fib of 7 is 13. 2 to the power 10 is 1024. Sum of digits of 4031 is 8. All three, correct.

scenes.animation: Drum hit; Xecxec counting on his claws
scenes.narration: Fibonacci's favourite food? Anything that adds up from the last two meals.

scenes.onScreen: `bug.c`: fib(40) with a call counter; 1.2 s pause; "Calls made: 331160281"; table of calls for n = 10, 20, 30, 40; loop fix
scenes.animation: Spinner while waiting; counter rolls up like a petrol pump; fix runs instantly, mint tick
scenes.narration: Today's bug: slow recursion. Our fib is correct, but watch what happens with fib of 40. We add a global counter, calls, that goes up by one every time fib runs. Run it, and wait. On our test machine it took about a second; your time will differ, and older laptops take longer. The answer: 102,334,155. And the counter: 331,160,281 calls. That's over 33 crore function calls for one number! Why? Remember the call tree: fib calls itself twice, and the same values get calculated again and again. Look at this table. fib of 10: 177 calls. fib of 20: 21,891. fib of 30: about 27 lakh. fib of 40: over 33 crore. Each step of 10 multiplies the work by more than 100. There's no error, no warning, just a program that seems frozen. The fix: when recursion repeats work, use a loop. Keep two variables, a and b, start them at 0 and 1, and step forward n times. fib of 40 now takes just 40 steps and finishes instantly. Recursion is beautiful, but it is not always fast. Later, in the algorithms module, you'll see a trick that keeps the recursion and remembers old answers.

scenes.onScreen: Challenge card: print Fibonacci numbers 0 to 20 using recursive fib
scenes.narration: Your challenge: print the first 21 Fibonacci numbers, from fib of 0 up to fib of 20, on one line, using the recursive fib from today. It's still fast for numbers this small. The last number should be 6765.

scenes.onScreen: Module 5 complete badge · Next: EP 41 · Arrays
scenes.narration: That's Module 5 complete! You can now write functions, pass values, split files, and think recursively. Next module: storing many values in one name. Arrays. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

Calls made: 331160281

| n | Calls |

bug.why: recursive fib recomputes the same smaller values again and again, so the number of calls grows explosively; a loop computes each value once.

shorts.title: 331 Million Function Calls
shorts.hook: the call counter rolling up past 300,000,000
shorts.script: This tiny Fibonacci function looks innocent. Ask it for fib of 40, and it makes 331 million calls. Why? It calls itself twice, and the same values get worked out again and again. fib of 10: 177 calls. fib of 40: 331 million. The same answer with a loop takes 40 steps.
shorts.caption: Correct code can still be terrible code.

shorts.title: The Recursion Recipe
shorts.hook: recipe card "3 questions for every recursion"
shorts.script: Three questions solve any recursion problem. What's the smallest case? How is my problem a smaller copy? How do I combine? Sum of digits: if n is 0, return 0. Otherwise, the last digit, n mod 10, plus the sum of digits of n divided by 10. 4031 becomes 1 plus 3 plus 0 plus 4. 8.
shorts.caption: Save this for your next C exam.

shorts.title: Slow Recursion Bug
shorts.hook: a frozen terminal with a spinner
shorts.script: No error. No warning. Your program just seems frozen. Recursive fib of 40 is making 331 million calls because it recalculates the same values over and over. Fix: a loop with two variables, a and b, starting at 0 and 1. Step forward n times. Same answer, 40 steps, instant.
shorts.caption: When recursion is the wrong tool.

shorts.title: Quiz: power(3, 4)
shorts.script: power returns 1 when exp is 0, otherwise base times power of base, exp minus 1. What is power of 3 and 4? A: 12. B: 64. C: 81. The answer is C: 3 times 3 times 3 times 3 is 81.
shorts.caption: Comment your answer before the reveal.
